records.content: 40% of Liver Transplant Recipients Remain Unvaccinated Against Hepatitis B, Raising Risk of Severe Complications: Study A study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases found that only 60% of liver transplant recipients were vaccinated against hepatitis B virus (HBV), leaving 4 in 10 unprotected against potentially severe complications. Researchers from Baylor College of Medicine analyzed data from deceased-donor liver transplant recipients between September 2022 and June 2024 using the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database. Factors associated with lower vaccine uptake included older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, shorter waiting-list duration, and lower educational attainment. The findings highlight gaps in HBV vaccination coverage among liver transplant recipients and the need to improve pre-transplant vaccination practices. The study was conducted by Michael A. and colleagues. To estimate the viral hepatitis vaccination coverage rates at the national level and the clinicodemographic characteristics associated with lack of vaccination, scientists from the Baylor College of Medicine carried out a retrospective cohort study based on the analysis of national registry data. Researchers obtained data from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry that included all adults who received liver transplantation from a deceased donor within September 1, 2022, and June 30, 2024. The research team studied immunization history, region, cause of liver disease, waitlist time, age, and socioeconomic status of patients. Key findings: - Results from the data analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing database for the period of 22 months showed large gaps in vaccination, along with clear demographic differences. - Less than 59.9% of patients who had received liver transplants using deceased donor organs from September 1, 2022, to June 30, 2024, had been fully immunized for the hepatitis B virus. - This means that about 40% of patients were not vaccinated prior to transplantation. Immunity levels varied geographically throughout transplant regions of the country. - Vaccination levels were independently linked to advanced age and low educational level of the patients. - The presence of alcohol-related liver disease and short waiting list times were also independent predictors of vaccination. In summary, empirical data from the UNOS registry highlight important gaps in pre-transplant preventive care in terms of lack of protection against hepatitis B virus among 40 percent of patients receiving livers. The findings of the study clearly indicate the importance of implementing multilevel interventions along with new vaccines to ensure the immunization of high-risk populations. Researchers at the University of São Paulo examined nearly 29,000 adult cancer patients treated at a major quaternary oncology center between 2010 and 2023 and found that the proportion carrying antibodies indicating past or present HBV infection dropped from 16.5 percent to 9.9 percent over the study period. The decline, reported in the journal Cancer Causes & Control, is encouraging evidence that vaccination and changing screening practices are reshaping the viral landscape faced by oncologists. Yet the same data reveal stubborn gaps: men, older adults, and non-White patients continue to bear a disproportionate burden of previous HBV exposure, and a substantial share of admitted cancer patients were never tested at all. The clinical stakes of this epidemiology are considerable. Hepatitis B virus infects hepatocytes and can establish a chronic infection that progresses to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; infection is recognized as one of the strongest risk factors for liver cancer, raising the odds of that malignancy by roughly 47-fold. Globally, an estimated 240 million people live with chronic HBV infection. For cancer patients, the virus carries an additional threat: systemic anticancer therapies suppress immune function, which can permit viral replication to resume even in patients whose infection appeared resolved. This reactivation is driven by covalently closed circular DNA, a persistent viral reservoir that remains within the nucleus of hepatocytes long after serological recovery. A recent global meta-analysis estimated reactivation rates of approximately 10 percent among patients with hematological malignancies and 5 percent among those with solid tumors. Reactivation is not a benign event. It can force interruption, delay, or modification of cancer treatment precisely when therapy is most needed, and it may culminate in acute hepatitis, liver failure, and death. For this reason, international guidelines recommend screening for HBV before patients begin chemotherapy or other immunosuppressive regimens. Patients who test positive for the hepatitis B surface antigen should receive antiviral therapy with agents such as entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, or tenofovir alafenamide, while those who are surface-antigen negative but positive for antibody against the core antigen, known as anti-HBc, should be considered at risk of reactivation and managed with antiviral prophylaxis or serological and molecular monitoring. Despite these recommendations, screening remains inconsistently implemented across oncology centers worldwide. The São Paulo study drew on laboratory records from the São Paulo State Cancer Institute, affiliated with the Clinical Hospital of the university’s Faculty of Medicine, which has treated more than 140,000 cancer patients since opening in 2008. Of 125,985 patients admitted between 2010 and 2023, 28,869, or 22.9 percent, underwent anti-HBc testing. The mean age of those tested was 56 years, roughly two-thirds were women, and 61.4 percent self-identified as White. Solid tumors accounted for 71.2 percent of the cohort, with breast cancer the most common diagnosis, while hematological malignancies made up 22.2 percent, led by non-Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma. HBV exposure was defined as anti-HBc positivity, a marker that indicates prior contact with the virus but does not by itself distinguish resolved infection from active disease. The headline finding is a statistically significant downward trend in seroprevalence, from 16.5 percent in 2010 to 9.9 percent in 2023. The decline was broad but uneven. Among men, seroprevalence fell from 25.1 percent to 12.3 percent, a steeper drop than among women, whose rates fell from 11.4 percent to 8.3 percent. Every age group improved, including patients aged 18 to 39, whose seroprevalence fell from 7.7 percent to 2.4 percent, and those aged 60 and older, whose rates declined from 20.1 percent to 13.7 percent. Seroprevalence also fell significantly among White patients and among those with solid tumors. By contrast, no significant trend emerged among non-White individuals, whose rates moved only from 21.4 percent to 17.7 percent, or among patients with hematological malignancies, whose rates remained essentially flat at around 13 percent. Multivariable logistic regression sharpened the demographic picture. Patients aged 60 or older had 4.4-fold higher odds of HBV exposure than those under 40, men had 89 percent higher odds than women, and non-White patients had 25 percent higher odds than White patients. The age gradient likely reflects cumulative lifetime exposure in cohorts born before universal neonatal vaccination, compounded by the reduced immunogenicity of hepatitis B vaccines in older adults. The sex difference may have biological underpinnings: androgens exert immunosuppressive effects, while estrogens appear to enhance immune and vaccine responses, potentially leaving men less able to clear or control the virus. The ethnic disparity points toward inequities in social determinants of health, including unequal access to vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment, a pattern consistent with prior Brazilian and international studies. Cancer type itself was not independently associated with exposure, but subgroup patterns were striking. Among hematological malignancies, non-Hodgkin lymphoma showed a seroprevalence of 15.5 percent, a malignancy repeatedly linked to HBV in meta-analyses, though the mechanisms remain unresolved. Among solid tumors, the highest rates appeared in sarcoma, at 43.5 percent, a figure the authors caution may be inflated by small numbers, and in liver and bile duct cancers, at 31.2 percent. In adjusted analyses, liver and bile duct cancers carried more than threefold higher odds of HBV exposure, and gastrointestinal cancers carried 41 percent higher odds, findings consistent with the established oncogenic role of the virus, which operates through chronic hepatic inflammation, integration of viral DNA into the host genome, and the activity of viral proteins such as HBx. Within the anti-HBc-positive group, additional testing of subsets clarified the virological picture. The hepatitis B surface antigen was positive in 7.8 percent of those tested, indicating current infection, while 73.2 percent carried anti-HBs antibodies consistent with resolved infection. Among 484 patients who underwent HBV DNA testing, 25.6 percent had detectable viral load. Taken together, most anti-HBc-positive patients showed evidence of past exposure, but a meaningful minority carried molecular or serological signs of active infection, underscoring why confirmatory testing matters before immunosuppressive therapy begins. One encouraging operational trend accompanied the epidemiological one: the proportion of admitted patients screened for anti-HBc rose from 11.1 percent in 2010 to 29.2 percent in 2023. Even so, more than two-thirds of cancer patients admitted over the period were never tested, and global data suggest screening before chemotherapy reached only about 57 percent in pooled estimates, with uptake particularly weak among patients with solid tumors. The authors note that their retrospective, single-center design has limits, including incomplete medical records, unknown testing indications, and possible selection bias, and that treatment-related immunosuppression may have blunted antibody detectability in some patients. Still, the scale of the cohort and the length of the observation window lend weight to the conclusion. As vaccination coverage expands and screening becomes more systematic, the residual burden of HBV exposure among cancer patients should continue to shrink, provided that prevention reaches the demographic groups the data show are still being left behind. AusperBio to Present Long-Term Follow-Up Data of AHB-137 Treatment in Chronic Hepatitis B in Two Late-Breaking Oral Presentations at AASLD The Liver Meeting® 2026 PR Newswire Wed, October 7, 2026 at 8:30 PM EDT 4 min read Two abstracts on long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment for chronic hepatitis B have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026. SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AusperBio Therapeutics, Inc. and Ausper Biopharma Co., Ltd. (together, "AusperBio"), a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company, today announced that two abstracts reporting long-term follow-up data of AHB-137 treatment have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting® 2026, the annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD), to be held November 5–9 in Denver, Colorado, USA. AusperBio The presentations will report long-term follow-up from the AB-10-8004 study (NCT07146100) in two populations of participants with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who completed prior AHB-137 clinical studies: nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) treatment-experienced patients, and treatment-naïve patients who received AHB-137 monotherapy. "We are honored that two abstracts from the AB-10-8004 study have been selected for late-breaking oral presentations at The Liver Meeting®," said Chris Yang, Co-founder and CSO of AusperBio. "We look forward to sharing these long-term follow-up data with the hepatology community as we continue to advance AHB-137 toward our goal of a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B." The presentation details are as follows: Publication Number: 5001 Abstract Title: Durability of AHB-137 up to 9 Month Post End-of-Studies in Nucleos(t)ide Analogue Treated Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: First Long-Term Follow-up Report from the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 2:00 pm – 2:15 pm MT Presenter: Jinlin Hou, MD, Southern Medical University, Guangdong, China Publication Number: 5010 Abstract Title: Durability of Functional Cure to AHB-137 Monotherapy in Treatment-Naïve Participants with Chronic Hepatitis B: Long-Term Follow-Up Results of the AB-10-8004 Study Session: Late Breaking Abstract Parallel Session 2 Date and Time: November 8, 2026, 6:00 pm – 6:15 pm MT Presenter: Junqi Niu, MD, The First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China Late-breaking abstracts will be available on the AASLD website beginning at 8:00 am MT on November 5, 2026. AusperBio plans to issue a press release with additional details following the presentations. The full scientific program for The Liver Meeting® 2026, as well as the abstracts, can be found on the AASLD website. Story Continues About AHB-137 AHB-137 is AusperBio's lead investigational unconjugated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB), developed using the Company's proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO platform. AHB-137 is designed to suppress hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) production, inhibit viral DNA replication, and promote immune reactivation, with the goal of achieving a functional cure for CHB. AHB-137 has demonstrated promising clinical results and is currently being evaluated in a Phase 3 trial in China, following completion of a global Phase 1 study and multiple Phase 2 studies. The Company is advancing AHB-137 through a coordinated global development strategy toward potential commercialization. AHB-137 is an investigational product candidate and has not been approved by any regulatory authority. About AusperBio AusperBio is a near-commercial biopharmaceutical company focused on developing differentiated oligonucleotide therapeutics and targeted delivery technologies, with an initial focus on achieving a functional cure for chronic hepatitis B. The Company's innovation engine is built on its proprietary Med-OligoTM ASO and Au-HALOTM targeted delivery platforms, supporting the development of therapies across multiple oligonucleotide modalities. With multiple clinical-stage programs and a growing pipeline, AusperBio is advancing a backbone-based combination strategy for functional cure of CHB while exploring opportunities in additional disease areas with significant unmet medical needs. Risk of Severe Complications: Study Written By : Dr Riya Dave ,Medically Reviewed By : Dr. Kamal Kant Kohli Published On 2026-10-04T20:45:11+05:30 | Updated On 4 Oct 2026 8:45 PM IST A study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases found that only 60% of liver transplant recipients were vaccinated against hepatitis B virus (HBV), leaving 4 in 10 unprotected against potentially severe complications. Researchers from Baylor College of Medicine analyzed data from deceased-donor liver transplant recipients between September 2022 and June 2024 using the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) database. Factors associated with lower vaccine uptake included older age, alcohol-associated liver disease, shorter waiting-list duration, and lower educational attainment. The findings highlight gaps in HBV vaccination coverage among liver transplant recipients and the need to improve pre-transplant vaccination practices. The study was conducted by Michael A. and colleagues. To estimate the viral hepatitis vaccination coverage rates at the national level and the clinicodemographic characteristics associated with lack of vaccination, scientists from the Baylor College of Medicine carried out a retrospective cohort study based on the analysis of national registry data. Researchers obtained data from the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry that included all adults who received liver transplantation from a deceased donor within September 1, 2022, and June 30, 2024. The research team studied immunization history, region, cause of liver disease, waitlist time, age, and socioeconomic status of patients. Key findings: Results from the data analysis from the United Network for Organ Sharing database for the period of 22 months showed large gaps in vaccination, along with clear demographic differences. Less than 59.9% of patients who had received liver transplants using deceased donor organs from September 1, 2022, to June 30, 2024, had been fully immunized for the hepatitis B virus. This means that about 40% of patients were not vaccinated prior to transplantation. Immunity levels varied geographically throughout transplant regions of the country. Vaccination levels were independently linked to advanced age and low educational level of the patients. The presence of alcohol-related liver disease and short waiting list times were also independent predictors of vaccination. In summary, empirical data from the UNOS registry highlight important gaps in pre-transplant preventive care in terms of lack of protection against hepatitis B virus among 40 percent of patients receiving livers. The findings of the study clearly indicate the importance of implementing multilevel interventions along with new vaccines to ensure the immunization of high-risk populations. records.content: HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C Screening to Begin in Govt De-addiction Facilities Yudh Nashean Virudh is leading revolution towards a stronger, healthier and prosperous Punjab: Dr. Balbir Singh. Published on: Oct 5, 2026, 11:15:35 IST By Genesis Prefer HT on Google Share via Copy link Punjab’s fight against drug abuse and communicable diseases is strengthening with Triple H screening for HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C set to begin shortly in government de-addiction and rehabilitation facilities. Punjab launches triple H screening to combat drug abuse and infectious diseases. The decision is part of the Bhagwant Mann's Yudh Nashean Virudh initiative and aims to provide comprehensive treatment to people with substance-use disorders and prevent the spread of blood-borne infections in the state. Viral infections like HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C spread through risk behaviors like sharing needles and syringes, and detecting and treating these diseases is an important part towards reintegrating people suffering from addiction back in their communities. For years, screening camps for HIV and hepatitis were organised periodically, often at intervals of about two months. While these camps provided opportunities for testing, there was limited scope to track who had attended, who had missed the camp and who subsequently required follow-up. Under the new approach, screening will be linked directly to the de-addiction and rehabilitation process rather than relying primarily on periodic camps. This is expected to create more consistent opportunities for testing and facilitate referrals for individuals who require further investigation, treatment or continued medical care. Health and Family Welfare Minister Dr Balbir Singh said, “People with a history of injecting drug use face an increased risk of blood-borne infections, and that early detection is important for timely medical care and counselling.” He added, “Under the leadership of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, Yudh Nashean Virudh is leading a revolution towards a stronger, healthier and prosperous Punjab. Our goal is not simply to help people overcome addiction, but also to enable them to lead healthier lives and contribute to society. By integrating HIV, Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C screening into de-addiction services, the Government is taking another important step towards ensuring that recovery leads to a meaningful and brighter future.” Earlier, a person who missed a screening camp could remain outside the testing cycle until another camp was held weeks or months later. By linking testing with de-addiction services, the state can easily identify those who need to be screened and ensure that positive cases are referred for appropriate care. The decision reflects the state’s seriousness in battling the spread of infectious diseases in the state. Earlier in August, Dr. Balbir Singh announced adoption of advanced testing technologies, including Nucleic Acid Testing (NAT) and Chemiluminescence Immunoassay (CLIA), to enhance the early detection of transfusion-transmitted infections such as HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C and strengthen blood safety in Punjab. Diagnostic testing for the three infections can also be availed free-of-cost at all Aam Aadmi Clinics in the state. These infections can remain undetected for years because many infected individuals do not experience noticeable symptoms, even as the underlying disease progresses. Early diagnosis and treatment, however, can improve treatment outcomes and help patients to live long, healthy lives. The integration of Triple H screening also reflects a broader approach to substance-use treatment, recognising that recovery goes beyond withdrawal management and abstinence. Counselling, psychological support, medical care and social rehabilitation are all important components of sustained recovery, alongside the identification and management of associated health conditions. With the rollout already underway in private facilities and government centres expected to follow shortly, the initiative seeks to strengthen the continuum of care available to people affected by substance use. records.content: Press Releases Precision BioSciences Announces Late-Breaking Oral Presentation for PBGENE-HBV at AASLD The Liver Meeting 2026 October 8, 2026 | 9 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print DURHAM, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Precision BioSciences, Inc. (Nasdaq: DTIL), a clinical stage gene editing company utilizing its novel proprietary ARCUS® platform to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for high unmet need diseases, today announced that it has been selected to deliver a late-breaking oral presentation at The Liver Meeting 2026, the 77 th annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD). The Liver Meeting 2026 will take place November 5-9 in Denver, CO. Details of the oral presentation: Type of presentation: Late-breaking oral presentation Abstract title: Durable pgRNA loss in both HBeAg positive and negative patients treated with PBGENE-HBV supports path towards viral cure Presenter: Man-Fung Yuen Authors: Man-Fung Yuen, Anca Streinu Cercel, Vlad A. Ichim, Emily B. Harrison, James M. Harris, Keely Dulmage, Andrew Van Cott, Abhishek Chandiramani, Neil Leatherbury, Janel Lape, Peter Balfe, Jeff Smith, Cassandra L. Gorsuch, Stanley Frankel, Oby Sogbetun, Jane McKeating, Mark S. Sulkowski, Edward J. Gane Date and time: Sunday, November 8, 2026, 2:15PM-2:30PM MST Publication number: 5002 About PBGENE-HBV (Hepatitis B Viral Elimination Program): PBGENE-HBV is Precision’s wholly owned in vivo gene editing program being evaluated in ELIMINATE-B, a global clinical trial, as a potential curative treatment for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV is the only clinical stage program that targets and eliminates covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), the sole source of viral replication, leading to sustained loss of pregenomic RNA (pgRNA), the precursor for HBV DNA. PBGENE-HBV is the first and only in vivo gene elimination approach to prospectively employ repeat lipid nanoparticle (LNP) administration in chronic hepatitis B with the goal of viral cure, as measured by sustained undetectable HBV DNA off nucleos(t)ide therapy. The FDA has previously provided guidance that undetectable HBV DNA is a validated endpoint for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV has been granted Fast Track designation by the FDA. Further details on the trial can be found on Precision’s website and on clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06680232. About Hepatitis B: Chronic hepatitis B viral (HBV) infection causes inflammation and damage to the liver, leading to increased risk of death from liver cancer or cirrhosis. There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B, and current treatments rarely result in a functional cure, primarily due to persistence of viral DNA in the liver. In patients with chronic hepatitis B, cccDNA, which contains the full-length viral genome, persists long term, produces pgRNA, and is the sole source of new infectious viral particles. Since cccDNA is the only source of infectious particles (HBV DNA), we believe elimination of cccDNA could result in a viral cure of chronic hepatitis B. Sustained loss of HBV DNA alone as a result of cccDNA elimination is a validated endpoint for the FDA and highly relevant for PBGENE-HBV. About the ELIMINATE-B Trial: The Phase 1 ELIMINATE-B study is currently enrolling both HBeAg negative and positive chronic hepatitis B patients at world-class sites in the United States, Europe, Asia and Oceania. The goal of the study is to define the optimal dose and number of dose administrations for safely eliminating cccDNA. Precision continues to accelerate recruitment and evaluate a genetically diverse patient population in the Phase 1 study. About Precision BioSciences, Inc. Precision BioSciences, Inc. is a clinical stage gene editing company dedicated to improving life (DTIL) with its novel and proprietary ARCUS ® genome editing platform that differs from other technologies in the way it cuts, its smaller size, and its simpler structure. These features are intended for ARCUS nucleases to drive more defined therapeutic outcomes. Using ARCUS, the Company’s pipeline is comprised of clinical stage in vivo gene editing candidates designed to deliver lasting cures for the broadest range of genetic and infectious diseases where no adequate treatments exist. For more information about Precision BioSciences, please visit www.precisionbiosciences.com . The ARCUS ® platform is being used to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for sophisticated gene edits, including gene elimination (removing a viral genome e.g. viral DNA such as in the Company’s PBGENE-HBV program), and excision (removing a large portion of a defective gene by delivering two ARCUS nucleases in a single AAV such as in the Company’s PBGENE-DMD program) and gene insertion (inserting DNA into a gene to cause expression or add function). records.content: Manila Bulletin Opinion Vaccine-preventable cancers Opinion Vaccine-preventable cancers By Raymundo W. Lo, MD, FPSP UNDER THE MICROSCOPE You read that right. Apart from vaccines treating and curing cancers, they can actually prevent cancers! There are many viruses/bacteria that are known to cause cancer, either because they hijack the cell’s mechanisms for repairing cell damage, which then goes on to cause genetic mutations that cause cancer, or the organisms themselves are oncogenic, meaning they can cause cancers to develop. A study by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) in 2024 showed that one in eight cancers worldwide are believed to be caused by infections. That’s about 2.3 million (12 percent) of new cancer cases each year. That’s the same fraction as lung cancer in all cancers in the USA alone. Some cancer researchers believe the IARC’s estimate to be very conservative. What are these organisms and what cancers do they cause? The highest number of cancers caused by infections is gastric cancer, and the trigger is Helicobacter pylori infection. Almost 800,000 cases of gastric cancer occur annually. Though there are no vaccines yet for H. pylori, it can be detected by gastroscopy and treated with antibiotics. It is followed by the Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), which causes 750,000 cervical, anal, vulvar, penile cancers as well as head and neck cancers worldwide. Next is hepatitis B virus which is linked to around 360,000 cases of liver cancer worldwide, with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) responsible for 260,000 cases globally, mainly nasopharyngeal cancer, some gastric cancers, and Hodgkins lymphoma. Hepatitis C virus was responsible for 160,000 liver cancer cases worldwide. HIV is another virus that can cause cancers, due to the profound immunosuppression it causes. Typical tumors include Kaposi sarcoma, anal cancer, lung cancer, non-Hodgkins lymphoma, liver cancer, cervical cancer and head and neck cancers. Fortunately, new medications can now reduce HIV viral loads to zero, thus reducing the possibility of developing these cancers. The higher burden of infection-caused cancer cases is in the less-developed countries in Eastern Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa, Central and Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia. Here in the Philippines, we have high rates of infection for hepatitis B virus. The figures I gathered in the 1990s showed about 75 percent of Filipinos had been exposed to HBV with 15-20 percent carrier status, meaning they were living with HBV in their bodies and had a high risk of developing liver cancer, which is very deadly. Early vaccination of babies decreased hepatitis B carriers (0.8 percent among five to six year-olds in 2018) compared to 16.7 percent among adults in the pre-vaccination era. But liver cancer is still the fourth most common cancer type and the second most common cause of cancer deaths. Taiwan used to have many liver cancers but the incidence has dropped due to a very successful early HBV vaccination program. We also have high rates of cervical and nasopharyngeal cancers locally due to HPV, and now we have effective vaccines for this virus. The DOH has a campaign to vaccinate 12-year-old females against HPV but we have yet to see the results. It should also be given to young boys as they can infect the girls via sexual intercourse and both sexes can develop nasopharyngeal and other HPV-associated cancers. My column, “A new approach to cervical cancer screening” (March 12, 2024) proposed a viable path toward more women to be screened for HPV and early cervical cancer. Now, we have many effective tools for these infections, including vaccination (HBV and HPV), testing (H. pylori, HPV, HCV, HBV, HIV) screening, diagnosis and treatment of these cancer-causing infections. The key challenges are limited access to and uptake of these measures due to financial constraints and lack of political commitment. Social stigma related to infections (HIV, HPV) also play a role in preventing access to interventions. The IARC scientists said governments should prioritize scaling up these interventions to prevent transmission of these infections and prevent many infection-caused cancers. Top priority goes to highly effective vaccines and screening and treatment of persistent infections. So, why are vaccines taking the limelight now even as anti-vaxxer sentiment is on the rise worldwide? It’s because vaccines are highly effective in preventing infections for which vaccines are available. They act much in the same way the body responds to infections, which is to stimulate our immune systems to rev up our immune defenses against invaders. Now, vaccines are being employed to combat cancers, which are actually our own cells gone rogue. Most cancers have genetic mutations that set them apart from benign cells, and these mutations tend to evade the immune system. Cancer vaccines help our immune systems recognize the cancer cells and kill them. With the advent of immunotherapy for cancers, we are now making great strides in controlling a once formidable enemy. Vaccines against infections that cause cancers, and now directly against cancers are here to stay. It’s the wave of the future. records.content: Home News Trending Celebrity Biography History Beauty Fashion Health Fitness Living Food Moms How Tos Money Business Career Opportunities Shop Fabwoman Amazon Store Product Reviews Relationships Marriage Weddings Insights From HPV to Hepatitis: 5 Infections That Can Increase Your Risk Of Cancer October 8, 2026Posted byby Anu Do you know that infections are the leading cause of cancer? Cancer, as we all know, has become a very common health issue, with millions of new cases springing up every day globally. According to a new study published in the journal The Lancet Oncology, about 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections, many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening, or straightforward treatments. The study also found that about 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses. The five leading infections were human papillomavirus (HPV), Helicobacter pylori, hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and hepatitis C. 1. Human papillomavirus (HPV) Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a common sexually transmitted infection spread through intimate skin-to-skin contact, including vaginal, anal, or oral sex. It can spread even when an infected person has no visible signs or symptoms. Condoms can reduce the risk of transmission but do not provide complete protection because HPV can infect areas of skin that are not covered by a condom. According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), HPV was responsible for approximately 750,000 cancer cases globally in 2024, making it one of the world’s leading infection-related causes of cancer. About 600,000 of these cases were cervical cancers. Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to prevent HPV-related cancers, while regular cervical cancer screening and checkups remain important. 2. Helicobacter pylori (H.pylori) Helicobacter pylori, commonly called H. pylori, is a bacterium that infects the stomach. H. pylori is a bacterial infection that infects the stomach and is a major cause of stomach issues such as ulcers and gastritis. It is usually spread through saliva, vomit, or stool. Chronic H. pylori infection can lead to inflammation and damage the stomach lining, increasing the risk of stomach (gastric) cancer. It is also associated with a type of lymphoma called MALT lymphoma. 760,000 new cancer cases in 2024 were attributable to H. pylori, according to IARC, making it the largest infection-related cause of cancer globally. Most of these cancers were stomach cancers. H. pylori infection can be treated with antibiotics, which can significantly reduce the risk of stomach cancer. 3. Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) Hepatitis B (HBV) is a virus that infects the liver and, if infection becomes chronic, it can cause inflammation and damage that may eventually lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer. It usually spreads when a person comes into contact with infected blood or certain body fluids. The latest IARC analysis estimates that HBV was responsible for approximately 360,000 cases of liver cancer globally in 2024. Because hepatitis B often causes no symptoms, infected people may not know they have it; therefore, vaccination offers the best protection. 4. Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a common virus estimated to infect about 95% of the world’s population and usually causes no serious long-term problems. While most people infected with EBV never develop cancer, the virus is associated with several cancers, including Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and most recently stomach cancers. IARC’s latest estimates put the number of EBV-attributable cancer cases at approximately 260,000 worldwide in 2024, making it the fourth-largest infectious cause of cancer globally. There is currently no licensed vaccine for the treatment of EBV. 5. Hepatitis C (HCV) Similar to Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C (HCV) is a virus that primarily attacks the liver. If untreated, chronic hepatitis C can cause liver inflammation, fibrosis, and cirrhosis, leading to an increase in the risk of liver cancer. HCV is also associated with some cases of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. IARC estimates that approximately 160,000 new cancer cases globally in 2024 were attributable to hepatitis C. Unlike hepatitis B, there is currently no vaccine for hepatitis C. However, a short course of antiviral drugs can cure more than 95% of infections and substantially reduce people’s risk of developing liver cancer. Further details on the trial can be found on Precision's website and on clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06680232. About Hepatitis B: Chronic hepatitis B viral (HBV) infection causes inflammation and damage to the liver, leading to increased risk of death from liver cancer or cirrhosis. There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B, and current treatments rarely result in a functional cure, primarily due to persistence of viral DNA in the liver. In patients with chronic hepatitis B, cccDNA, which contains the full-length viral genome, persists long term, produces pgRNA, and is the sole source of new infectious viral particles. Close Vaccines Older Adults Need: What to Get, When to Get It, and Why It Matters Vaccine Information and Resources Oct 05, 2026 8 min read Print Page Share Dorothea VafiadisNCOA Senior Strategist for Healthy Aging Vaccines play an important role in helping older adults stay healthy, active, and independent as they age. Staying on top of recommended vaccines is one more way to take care of yourself and keep doing the things you enjoy. There are several vaccines worth knowing about, from your annual flu shot to vaccines that help protect against shingles, pneumococcal disease, RSV, COVID-19, and hepatitis B. Medicare covers recommended vaccines at no cost when you meet the coverage requirements for your Medicare plan. Read on to learn who should get each vaccine, when to get it, and how Medicare covers it. At a Glance: Vaccines Older Adults Need Vaccine Who should get it? How often? Medicare coverage Flu All adults Every year Part B Shingles (Shingrix) Adults 50+ 2 doses (2–6 months apart) Part D Pneumococcal Adults 50+ (per CDC guidance) Usually 1 dose Part B RSV Adults 75+; adults 50–74 at increased risk One dose Part D COVID-19 All adults (talk to your provider first) As recommended Part B Hepatitis B Adults with risk factors 2–4 doses, depending on vaccine Part B (eligible adults) What vaccines do seniors need? Below is a list of six recommended vaccines for older adults. Medicare covers recommended adult vaccines at no cost when you meet the coverage requirements and receive the vaccine from an appropriate Medicare-participating provider or pharmacy. 1. Flu vaccine Who should get the flu vaccine? According to current Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommendations, everyone age 6 months and older should get a flu vaccine every year, with very few exceptions. Several flu vaccine options are available for older adults, including high-dose, adjuvanted, recombinant, and mRNA vaccines. For the 2026–2027 flu season, adults age 50 and older also have the option of mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA flu vaccine approved in the U.S. Talk with your health care provider about which flu vaccine is right for you. Why is the flu vaccine important for older adults? Older people, especially the 93% of adults age 65+ who are managing at least one chronic condition, are more likely to develop complications or become hospitalized with the flu. Flu combined with pneumonia—a common acute condition among the aging population—consistently ranks as one of the top 12 causes of death in the U.S. According to CDC, the flu shot prevents millions of illnesses and doctor's visits each year. Getting the shot doesn’t guarantee you won’t get sick—but it does help lower the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and complications. That protection matters, even in challenging flu seasons where the vaccine isn’t a perfect match to circulating strains. When should get the flu vaccine? You should get a flu shot annually. Flu season in the U.S. typically peaks between November and March, so aim to get your vaccine in September or October to prevent contracting the flu from a family member, friend, or caregiver during the holidays. It’s important to note that it takes about two weeks for the vaccine to provide protection. Did you miss the prime vaccination window? Flu season can peak as late as February or even March—so as long as the virus is still circulating, it’s not too late to get your yearly flu shot. How does Medicare cover the flu vaccine? Medicare Part B covers one flu shot each flu season at no cost when you get it from a provider or pharmacy that accepts Medicare assignment. You don't need a Part D plan to receive this coverage. If you have original Medicare, you must use a physician or health care provider who accepts Medicare. If you have Medicare Advantage, you may have to use an in-network doctor or pharmacy. Contact your plan for details. 2. Shingles vaccine (Shingrix) Who should get the shingles vaccine? CDC recommends that healthy adults age 50 years and older get two doses of the vaccine to prevent shingles (Shingrix) separated by two to six months. Vaccination is also recommended for some adults age 19 and older who have compromised immune systems. People who are immunocompromised can receive their second dose of Shingrix one to two months after the first dose. Note: Shingrix replaced the prior shingles vaccine Zostavax and has been the only shingles vaccine available in the U.S. since November 2020. If you had the Zostavax vaccine previously, you should still get the Shingrix shot. Talk to your health care provider about the best timing to get Shingrix. Why is the shingles vaccine important for older adults? Age-related decline in immunity can trigger the “reawakening” of the dormant chickenpox virus, according to researchers. One in three adults contracts shingles at some point in their life—the majority of whom are 60 years or older. The older you are when you get shingles, the more likely you are to have severe side effects, like fever, exhaustion, and loss of appetite. These can lead to malnutrition, physical deterioration, and/or additional infections. Whether you remember having chickenpox as a child or not, you should still talk to your doctor about getting vaccinated. When should you get the shingles vaccine? You should get the shingles vaccine as soon as you become eligible; there's no need to wait for a certain time of year to get vaccinated. The shingles shot is given in two doses, usually 2–6 months apart, to help protect against shingles and its complications. How does Medicare cover the shingles vaccine? The shingles vaccine is covered under Medicare Part D. If you have Medicare Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan with prescription drug coverage, you should pay nothing out of pocket when you receive this vaccination. You'll typically need to get the vaccine from a pharmacy or provider in your Part D plan's network. 3. Pneumococcal vaccine Who should get the pneumococcal vaccine? CDC guidelines recommend pneumococcal vaccination for all adults age 50 and older and for younger adults with certain medical conditions or other risk factors. There are several pneumococcal vaccines available for adults, including PCV15, PCV20, PCV21, and PPSV23. The vaccine and number of doses you need depend on your age, health, and vaccination history. Talk with your health care provider about which pneumococcal vaccine is right for you. Why is the pneumococcal vaccine important for older adults? Older adults and people with certain underlying conditions are at greater risk for severe pneumococcal-related illness and complications. Pneumococcal disease can cause pneumonia (infection of the lungs), meningitis (infection of the lining of the brain and spinal cord), and bacteremia (infection of the bloodstream), potentially leading to deafness, brain damage, loss of limbs, and even death. Each year, more than 2 million people develop a pneumococcal infection, and about 6,000 die from the disease.1 When should you get the pneumococcal vaccine? You can get the pneumococcal vaccine any time of year. According to CDC guidance, adults age 50 and older should receive the vaccine. But the timing and number of doses you need depend on your age, health, and vaccination history. Check with your doctor to see if you’ve had either pneumococcal vaccine already. How does Medicare cover the pneumococcal vaccine? The pneumococcal vaccine is a cost-free benefit covered by Medicare Part B. If you have Medicare Part B, you must use a physician or health care provider who accepts Medicare. If you have Medicare Advantage, you may have to use an in-network doctor or pharmacy. 4. RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) Who should get the RSV vaccine? CDC recommends the single-dose RSV vaccine for all adults age 75 and older and for adults ages 50–74 who are at increased risk for severe RSV disease due to certain chronic medical conditions or other risk factors. Three vaccines are currently approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to help prevent severe RSV in adults: GSK's Arexvy, Moderna's mResvia, and Pfizer's Abrysvo single-dose vaccines. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if the vaccine is right for you. Why is the RSV vaccine important? RSV, a common and highly contagious respiratory virus, can cause serious illness in older adults, especially those over 60 or with underlying health conditions like heart or lung disease. The infection can lead to pneumonia, hospitalization, and even death. Getting the RSV vaccine helps reduce the risk of dangerous complications. When should you get the RSV vaccine? You can get the RSV vaccine at any time, but late summer or early fall is the best time to get it. Keep in mind the RSV vaccine is not something you need every year. If you've already received an RSV vaccine, you don't need another dose at this time. How does Medicare cover the RSV vaccine? Medicare covers the RSV vaccine through Medicare Part D. If you have a standalone Part D plan or Medicare Advantage plan with prescription drug coverage, you should pay nothing out of pocket for this shot, but you may have to use an in-network doctor or pharmacy. Contact your plan for details. If you only have Medicare Part B and do not have Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan that includes prescription drug coverage, Medicare generally does not cover the RSV vaccine. You may have to pay the full cost out of pocket. 5. COVID-19 vaccine Who should get the COVID vaccine? CDC recommends that adults talk with their health care provider about whether COVID-19 vaccination is right for them based on their age, health conditions, and individual risk. Older adults and people with certain underlying health conditions remain at higher risk for severe COVID-19. NCOA encourages older adults to talk to their doctor about their personal risks and get vaccinated to protect their health, independence, and quality of life. Why is the COVID vaccine important? COVID-19 continues to pose the greatest risk to older adults. From 2022 to 2024, adults age 65 and older represented less than one-fifth of the U.S. population but accounted for nearly half of all COVID-19 cases, two-thirds of hospitalizations, and more than 80% of deaths.2 Due to a natural decline in immunity as we age, older adults face a greater risk of getting infected with COVID and developing severe complications. This is especially true for those with other health conditions (e.g., diabetes, obesity, cancer), those who’ve never received a COVID vaccine, and those living in long-term care facilities. When should you get the COVID vaccine? Ask your health care provider about the optimal timing of your COVID shot based on the time of year, your last vaccination, and any recent COVID infections. How does Medicare cover the COVID vaccine? Medicare covers the COVID vaccine through Medicare Part B. If you have original Medicare, you will pay nothing out of pocket as long as you visit a doctor or pharmacy that accepts Medicare assignment. If you have a Medicare Advantage plan, you generally must get the vaccine from a health care provider or pharmacy that is in your plan's network. 6. Hepatitis B vaccine Who should get the Hepatitis B vaccine? CDC recommends hepatitis B vaccination for all adults ages 19–59 and for adults age 60 and older who have certain risk factors. Adults age 60 and older without known risk factors may also choose to get vaccinated after talking with their health care provider. The hepatitis B vaccine is typically given in a series of two or three injections, depending on the specific vaccine. Once you've completed the recommended series, you generally don't need a booster. Why is the Hepatitis B vaccine important? Hepatitis B (or hep B) is a contagious virus that infects the liver. The liver and its function change as we age, making hep B more prevalent among older adults. Your risk of contracting hepatitis B increases if you have hemophilia, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), diabetes, or other conditions that lower resistance to infection. Acute hep B is particularly dangerous for older adults because there is no specific treatment for the symptoms. When should you get the Hepatitis B vaccine? Most Americans are vaccinated against hepatitis B as infants. If you are not sure if you’ve been vaccinated or if you are in a situation where you may need to update your vaccination, talk to your doctor. How does Medicare cover the Hepatitis B vaccine? Medicare Part B insurance covers the full cost of the hep B vaccine if: A doctor determines you are at high or medium risk of contracting the hep B virus, and The physician or health care provider administering the vaccine accepts Medicare. Talk to your doctor to determine your risk of getting hepatitis B. Make a plan to get vaccinated today Getting vaccinated is an important part of staying healthy and active as you age—and it also helps protect the health of your friends and family. If you have Medicare, you may pay nothing for recommended vaccines depending on the type of coverage you have. Check with your Medicare plan for specific coverage details and requirements. Sources 1. According to a new global epidemiological analysis, these carcinogenic infections accounted for approximately 12 percent of all newly diagnosed malignancies. The study evaluated twelve oncogenic pathogens , including viruses, a bacterium, and parasites, demonstrating that infection control holds an essential role in lowering the global cancer burden. Primary Pathogens Driving Infection-Related Cancers. Among the twelve evaluated infectious agents, five pathogens were responsible for nearly all infection-related cancers worldwide. Helicobacter pylori produced the highest cancer burden, causing an estimated 760,000 cases in 2024. Human papillomavirus followed closely, accounting for approximately 750,000 cases. Hepatitis B virus caused roughly 360,000 malignancies, while hepatitis C virus was linked to about 160,000 cases. Epstein-Barr virus emerged as the fourth leading infectious cause of malignancy globally, generating approximately 260,000 cases and surpassing hepatitis C virus. This placement reflects accumulating evidence showing that Epstein-Barr virus drives not only nasopharyngeal cancer and lymphomas but also a proportion of gastric cancers. The analysis also evaluated human immunodeficiency virus, Merkel cell polyomavirus, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, Schistosoma haematobium, Opisthorchis viverrini, and Clonorchis sinensis. Global Inequities and Infection Prevention Priorities. The surveillance data demonstrated marked geographical disparities in infection-related cancers. Eastern Asia shouldered 42 percent of all infection-attributable cancer cases globally, driven primarily by Helicobacter pylori and hepatitis B virus. The disease burden was also pronounced in Sub-Saharan Africa, where human papillomavirus and Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus predominated and were compounded by human immunodeficiency virus. More than three-quarters of all infection-related cancers developed in low- and middle-income countries, where clinical access to prevention and therapies remains unequal. Most of these malignancies remain preventable through established interventions, including vaccination against human papillomavirus and hepatitis B virus, screening programs, targeted antimicrobial therapy for Helicobacter pylori, and viral hepatitis treatment. Addressing persistent health-system barriers and investing in novel vaccines against Epstein-Barr virus will be vital to reducing future cancer incidence. Reference. Rumgay H et al. Connecting Cancer Survivors with Practical Resources Shannon Miller, CEO of Salto Health, joined Ryan Schmelz on LiveNOW from FOX to discuss empowering cancer survivors during recovery. The Brief About 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024 — roughly 12% of all new cases — were linked to infections, according to an IARC study. H. pylori and HPV caused the largest share of infection-related cancers, followed by hepatitis B, Epstein-Barr and hepatitis C viruses. More than three-quarters of these cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, though many can be prevented through vaccination, screening and treatment. LYON, France - A new study reveals that an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 – about 12% of all new cancer cases – were caused by infections. The analysis from the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) is based on cancer burden estimates from the IARC Global Cancer Observatory database. Study’s findings Big picture view: Published on Sept. 28 in The Lancet Oncology, the researchers estimated new cancer cases attributable to 12 infectious agents known to cause cancer in humans, including viruses, a bacterium and parasites. These 12 agents were: Helicobacter pylori, human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), EBV, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), Schistosoma haematobium, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), Opisthorchis viverrini, Clonorchis sinensis, Merkel cell polyomavirus, and HIV. About 2.3 million cancer cases worldwide in 2024 — roughly 12% of all new cases — were linked to infections, according to an IARC study. (Credit: Getty Images) The greatest cancer burden was linked to H. pylori, which was responsible for an estimated 760,000 cancer cases in 2024, closely followed by HPV, with 750,000 cases. In addition, HBV accounted for about 360,000 cases, EBV for approximately 260,000 cases, and HCV for about 160,000 cases. Together, the five infectious agents accounted for almost all cancers caused by infections. What they're saying: "The findings underscore the major role that infection control can play in reducing the global cancer burden," Dr. Harriet Rumgay, a scientist in the Cancer Surveillance Branch at IARC and a co-author of the article, said in a statement. "Despite progress in vaccination and screening, infection-related cancers remain a major global challenge, with the burden falling disproportionately on populations in low- and middle-income countries." Geographical inequalities Dig deeper: The study also revealed geographical inequalities. Eastern Asia accounted for 42% of all infection-attributable cancers worldwide, largely driven by H. pylori and HBV. The burden was also particularly high in Sub-Saharan Africa, driven by HPV and KSHV and worsened by HIV. More than three-quarters of infection-related cancers occurred in low- and middle-income countries, where access to prevention and treatment remains unequal, the agency noted. Analysis shows infection-related cancers continue to evolve Why you should care: EBV is the fourth largest infectious cause of cancer globally, ahead of HCV. This reflects growing evidence that EBV contributes not only to nasopharyngeal cancer and lymphomas but also to a proportion of gastric cancers. "This updated analysis shows that the landscape of infection-related cancers continues to evolve as scientific evidence advances," said Dr. Gary Clifford, a senior co-author of the study. "It also highlights where future investments in new prevention tools could have the greatest impact, particularly for infections such as EBV, for which effective vaccines are not yet available." IARC said most infection-related cancers can already be prevented through well-established public health measures, including vaccination against HPV and HBV, testing and treatment for H. pylori and viral hepatitis, HIV prevention and care, and screening programmes for HPV-related cancers. However, the agency said these interventions remain underused in many parts of the world because of persistent financial, political and health-system barriers. Study limitations The study had several limitations, the researchers acknowledged. Because the study used population-level estimates rather than tracking individual patients over time, the results depended on the quality of available cancer data in each country. Additionally, it only included infections already proven to cause cancer, so the total impact could be underestimated. Despite the findings, Dr. Joshua Cohen, medical director of the Gynecologic Cancer Program of City of Hope Orange County in Irvine, California, told Fox News Digital that "most cancers are not caused by infection." "We know that there are certain infections that we are exposed to over our lifetime that may result in an increased risk of certain cancers," Cohen said. RELATED: 7 everyday mistakes could be quietly damaging your vision, eye doctor warns "However, most cancers are not caused by infection." HPV is one of the most common drivers of cancers that arise along the rectum, vagina or cervix, as well as the oropharynx (back of the throat), according to Cohen, who was not involved in the study. "Eighty percent of the population has been exposed to certain types of HPV strains," he said. "About 40,000 people in the U.S. are diagnosed with these cancers each year." For most people who are exposed to HPV, the body will clear the virus on its own, Cohen said. "We don't know why some patients' immune systems allow them to clear the HPV infection and some don't." Another very common cancer, although less so in the U.S., is gastric cancer, he noted, which is linked to H. Pylori, an infection in the stomach. "We don't screen everybody for H. pylori in the U.S. – it's more common in other parts of the world, like Southeast Asia." However, those who have peptic ulcer disease or significant epigastric pain should talk with a gastroenterologist about getting screened and treated for H. pylori, the doctor advised. Lancet Study Links 1 in 8 Cancer Cases to Infections - Video Published On 3 Oct 2026 2:30 AM | Updated On 3 Oct 2026 2:30 AM Overview Infections were linked to an estimated 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024, accounting for about 12% of all cancer cases, according to a study published in The Lancet Oncology. This means around one in eight cancers diagnosed globally that year was associated with an infection. Researchers from the International Agency for Research on Cancer analysed cancer data involving 12 infectious agents known to cause cancer. Five infections accounted for almost all infection-related cases: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), human papillomavirus (HPV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV). H. pylori was linked to around 760,000 cases, mainly stomach cancer, making it the largest contributor. HPV was associated with approximately 750,000 cases and is the main cause of cervical cancer, while also contributing to several other cancers. HBV was linked to about 360,000 cases, primarily liver cancer. EBV accounted for around 260,000 cases, including some stomach cancers, nasopharyngeal cancers and lymphomas. HCV was associated with approximately 160,000 cases, mostly liver cancer. Infections do not mean cancer is inevitable. Risk depends on factors such as whether the infection persists, immune response and other individual risk factors. Long-term infections can cause inflammation or cellular damage that may contribute to cancer development over time. The burden was particularly high in low- and middle-income countries, which accounted for about 77% of infection-related cancers. Differences in infection prevalence, vaccination, screening, testing and treatment access may contribute to this gap. Several infection-related cancers can be prevented or reduced through public health measures. HPV and hepatitis B vaccination can lower cancer risk, while cervical screening can detect precancerous changes. Although there is no HCV vaccine, antiviral medicines can cure most infections. The findings highlight infection prevention, early detection and treatment as important components of global cancer prevention. (Nasdaq: DTIL), a clinical stage gene editing company utilizing its novel proprietary ARCUS® platform to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for high unmet need diseases, today announced that it has been selected to deliver a late-breaking oral presentation at The Liver Meeting 2026, the 77th annual meeting of the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD). The Liver Meeting 2026 will take place November 5-9 in Denver, CO. Details of the oral presentation: Type of presentation: Late-breaking oral presentation Abstract title: Durable pgRNA loss in both HBeAg positive and negative patients treated with PBGENE-HBV supports path towards viral cure Presenter: Man-Fung Yuen Authors: Man-Fung Yuen, Anca Streinu Cercel, Vlad A. Ichim, Emily B. Harrison, James M. Harris, Keely Dulmage, Andrew Van Cott, Abhishek Chandiramani, Neil Leatherbury, Janel Lape, Peter Balfe, Jeff Smith, Cassandra L. Gorsuch, Stanley Frankel, Oby Sogbetun, Jane McKeating, Mark S. Sulkowski, Edward J. Gane Date and time: Sunday, November 8, 2026, 2:15PM-2:30PM MST Publication number: 5002 About PBGENE-HBV (Hepatitis B Viral Elimination Program): PBGENE-HBV is Precision’s wholly owned in vivo gene editing program being evaluated in ELIMINATE-B, a global clinical trial, as a potential curative treatment for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV is the only clinical stage program that targets and eliminates covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), the sole source of viral replication, leading to sustained loss of pregenomic RNA (pgRNA), the precursor for HBV DNA. PBGENE-HBV is the first and only in vivo gene elimination approach to prospectively employ repeat lipid nanoparticle (LNP) administration in chronic hepatitis B with the goal of viral cure, as measured by sustained undetectable HBV DNA off nucleos(t)ide therapy. The FDA has previously provided guidance that undetectable HBV DNA is a validated endpoint for chronic hepatitis B. PBGENE-HBV has been granted Fast Track designation by the FDA. Further details on the trial can be found on Precision’s website and on clinicaltrials.gov under identifier NCT06680232. About Hepatitis B: Chronic hepatitis B viral (HBV) infection causes inflammation and damage to the liver, leading to increased risk of death from liver cancer or cirrhosis. There is no cure for chronic hepatitis B, and current treatments rarely result in a functional cure, primarily due to persistence of viral DNA in the liver. In patients with chronic hepatitis B, cccDNA, which contains the full-length viral genome, persists long term, produces pgRNA, and is the sole source of new infectious viral particles. Since cccDNA is the only source of infectious particles (HBV DNA), we believe elimination of cccDNA could result in a viral cure of chronic hepatitis B. Sustained loss of HBV DNA alone as a result of cccDNA elimination is a validated endpoint for the FDA and highly relevant for PBGENE-HBV. About the ELIMINATE-B Trial: The Phase 1 ELIMINATE-B study is currently enrolling both HBeAg negative and positive chronic hepatitis B patients at world-class sites in the United States, Europe, Asia and Oceania. The goal of the study is to define the optimal dose and number of dose administrations for safely eliminating cccDNA. Precision continues to accelerate recruitment and evaluate a genetically diverse patient population in the Phase 1 study. About Precision BioSciences, Inc. Precision BioSciences, Inc. is a clinical stage gene editing company dedicated to improving life (DTIL) with its novel and proprietary ARCUS® genome editing platform that differs from other technologies in the way it cuts, its smaller size, and its simpler structure. These features are intended for ARCUS nucleases to drive more defined therapeutic outcomes. Using ARCUS, the Company’s pipeline is comprised of clinical stage in vivo gene editing candidates designed to deliver lasting cures for the broadest range of genetic and infectious diseases where no adequate treatments exist. For more information about Precision BioSciences, please visit www.precisionbiosciences.com. The ARCUS® platform is being used to develop in vivo gene editing therapies for sophisticated gene edits, including gene elimination (removing a viral genome e.g. viral DNA such as in the Company’s PBGENE-HBV program), and excision (removing a large portion of a defective gene by delivering two ARCUS nucleases in a single AAV such as in the Company’s PBGENE-DMD program) and gene insertion (inserting DNA into a gene to cause expression or add function). 1 in 8 cancer cases worldwide are tied to these infections — most of them preventable Cancer Vaccines See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Human papilloma virus or HPV is one of several infections that scientists connected to about 2.3 million new cancer cases globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses. BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether. That’s according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology, which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments. “We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer,” said Gary Clifford, the study’s senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Ad Feedback “We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works,” Clifford said. “It’s an awareness-raising issue.” Related video CNN A simple blood test can detect 50 plus cancers. Here’s why that’s complicated 4:06 About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024. Other infections contributed substantially as well: Hepatitis B or HBV was linked to an estimated 360,000 cancer cases, which were mostly liver cancers. The Epstein-Barr virus or EBV was associated with about 260,000 cancer cases, of which a head and neck cancer starting in the nasopharynx was the main driver. Hepatitis C or HCV was tied to 160,000 cancer cases, mostly liver cancers. Related article This 2015 photo shows a pediatrician preparing a shot of the HPV vaccine for a patient in Cranston, Rhode Island. Keith Bedford/The Boston Globe/Getty Images/File What you need to know about the cancer-fighting HPV vaccine 5 min read “Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development,” Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email. “However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV,” Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available. Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory’s Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set. The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018, but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV. “EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma,” Clifford said. “That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we’ve identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas,” he said. “We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn’t really fully addressed because we didn’t understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing.” Where the infection-related cancer burden is greatest The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn’t evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment. But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives. Related article Drs Producoes/E+/Getty Images The HPV vaccine can reduce certain cancers by half. Expert explains why men and boys should get it 5 min read “Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later,” said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study. “Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States,” she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV. “Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer,” Fedirko said. “Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures.” How to ‘take away’ the risk Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference. Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops. Related article A new recommendation from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says all adults should be screened at least once in their lifetime for hepatitis B, an illness that's linked to liver disease and cancer. NIAID/CDC All adults should be screened for hepatitis B at least once, CDC says 2 min read Getting tested and following up with a doctor “almost takes away any cancer risk,” Clifford said. Once infections get diagnosed, “we know how to manage them,” he said. “The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we’re learning more about which ones, but that’s a work in progress. The point is: It doesn’t mean that you’ve got a cancer just because you have the infection.” For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road. The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop. Related article Papilloma virus, HPV). It causes cervical cancer. Image taken with transmission electron microscopy. (Photo by: BSIP/Universal Images Group via Getty Images) BSIP/Universal Images Group/Getty Images HPV vaccine reduced cervical cancer rates by 87% in women, UK study finds 3 min read Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection. HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses, which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer: cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection. The new research “teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer,” Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email. “This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced,” Lee said. “Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower.” Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include “safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis,” Rumgay said. “If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide.” Cancer Vaccines See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied!
